item.title: Shreveport Mayor Challenges 50 Cent To Deliver
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: 50 Cent's Shreveport criticism drew a response from Mayor Tom Arceneaux, who defended city support and sought a return call.
item.content:encoded:
Shreveport Mayor Tom Arceneaux challenged 50 Cent to deliver on his studio commitments, rejecting the rapper’s claim that City Hall had not backed him.

“Well, we have been most accommodating to Mr. Jackson from the very beginning, and now it’s time for him to perform,” Arceneaux told KSLA.

The mayor declined to comment on October 14, according to city communications director Leigh Anne Evensky.

Arceneaux said he wanted a return call and that no contract had been signed for the separate Red River District proposal. He said his call months earlier remained unanswered.

On “The Crew Has It,” 50 had questioned pouring more money into Shreveport without city support. He also said he still intended to do the work he had promised. He wanted recognition as a business owner and said earlier broken promises had made residents doubt new plans.

Red River is the city-owned entertainment area beneath the Texas Street Bridge. That proposal is separate from the larger studio plan. Inspections had found major repairs were needed there, and G-Unit wanted that work addressed before moving ahead.

The larger plan involved three sites, not just the riverfront entertainment area. Louisiana Economic Development’s January 12 announcement outlined more than $124 million in planned investment. Stageworks would be renovated for live events and production, Millennium Studios would be modernized, and a new dome-style immersive venue and park would be built downtown.

The state agreed to provide up to $50 million for eligible infrastructure and modernization work. That was performance-based support, tied to economic impact, local business involvement and delivery of the improvements.

An oversight body, the Shreveport Film & Entertainment Economic Development Corporation, was set up to work with the state agency on accountability for the project and its funds.

City Hall’s January 13 statement welcomed the state-backed plan while saying it required no additional municipal money. It put the estimated Millennium Studios investment at $78 million and Stageworks at $24 million, noting that both properties were leased to G-Unit.

There was already a separate Stageworks lease: the city and 50 signed it on June 6, 2025, for productions, events and multimedia work.

item.title: Warner Music Targets Film & TV Money With Licensing Shake-Up
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Warner Music Group moved to unite song-licensing teams, targeting film, TV, ad and game deals across its global catalog.
item.content:encoded:
Warner Music Group unveiled a plan to put one global boss in charge of its teams that license songs and recordings for films, TV shows, ads and games.

The company’s October 21 announcement promoted Ron Broitman to president of Global Sync. His team will span publisher Warner Chappell Music and label groups such as Atlantic Music Group and Warner Records Group.

Atlantic’s roster includes Cardi B, Missy Elliott and Jack Harlow.

Sync deals pair music with images. But a song and the recording of that song carry separate copyrights. A filmmaker who wants a specific recording generally needs permission for both the song and the master.

Warner said clients would have one place to seek licenses from its recording and publishing catalogs.

“We are making it easier and faster to license our entire global library,” Broitman said.

There is a growing pool of screen money at stake. The RIAA’s midyear report put U.S. recorded-music sync revenue at $231.8 million for the first half of 2026, up 18.2% from the same stretch last year. Those are industrywide wholesale receipts, not a tally of Warner’s earnings or artists’ take-home pay.

Warner Chappell CEO Guy Moot said the publisher’s team would remain part of the joint sync team to keep pitching its songwriters’ work.

Photo: Warner Music Santa Fe.jpg by Busition, via Wikimedia Commons. Cropped and resized; this image adaptation is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

item.title: Kurtis Blow & The D.O.C. Get Their Due At Paid In Full’s Vegas Gala
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Paid In Full Foundation will honor Kurtis Blow, The D.O.C., Nile Rodgers and Ralph McDaniels at its October 24 Las Vegas gala.
item.content:encoded:
The Paid In Full Foundation will put Kurtis Blow and The D.O.C. at the center of its next Hip Hop Grandmaster Awards, with a Las Vegas gala built around recognition and financial support for the people who helped create the culture.

The two MCs are the 2026 Grandmaster honorees for the October 24 event at the Bellagio. Nile Rodgers will receive the Quincy Jones Achievement Award, while Ralph McDaniels will receive the Contributor Award.

The foundation’s awards program pairs public honors with support for artists whose influence has not always brought matching financial rewards. The group says net proceeds from the gala will support that work, helping pioneers and other creatives pursue new projects.

Nas, Grandmaster Caz, Steve Stoute and Ben Horowitz discussed that mix of financial support and recognition in an a16z episode last month. Caz reflected on what the honor meant to his life and legacy.

This year’s honorees helped expand Hip-Hop in different ways. Kurtis Blow’s 1980 single “The Breaks” became the first gold-certified rap song. The D.O.C.’s platinum debut, “No One Can Do It Better,” arrived in 1989 through Ruthless Records, and his songwriting for N.W.A. and Dr. Dre extended his reach beyond his own records.

Rodgers’ connection runs through the music that early rappers built on. Chic’s “Good Times” provided the musical foundation for the Sugarhill Gang’s “Rapper’s Delight,” linking his work directly to rap’s early commercial breakthrough.

McDaniels helped give the culture a home on television. “Video Music Box” began in 1983, and New York City’s media office credited the host and producer with helping advance artists including LL Cool J and Jay-Z. In an AllHipHop interview last year, McDaniels also described the work of digitizing the show’s archive so those performances and interviews could reach new viewers.

The new group follows last year’s Bellagio honorees, including Kool G Rap, Grand Puba, Kool Rock Ski, Jalil Hutchins and George Clinton. Clinton’s recognition led to a memorable moment when he rapped “Follow The Leader” and Rakim joined him onstage.

The fourth annual gala is scheduled for Saturday, October 24, in the Bellagio’s Tower Ballroom.

Photo: Kurtis Blow im Musiktheater Bad (Hannover, Germany), 2012-03-30.JPG by Ferhat Ataman, via Wikimedia Commons. Cropped and resized; this image adaptation is licensed under CC BY-SA 3.0.

item.title: Sacha Baron Cohen Defends Ali G As Racism Debate Follows Movie Return
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Sacha Baron Cohen defended Ali G as a joke about white cultural theft, while critics questioned who really pays for the laugh.
item.content:encoded:
Sacha Baron Cohen defended Ali G against racism claims, arguing that the joke targeted a white man copying Black culture rather than the culture itself.

In a new TIME essay, Cohen called the character a fool whose borrowed style helps expose powerful people’s bias.

“The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him,” he wrote.

That defense speaks to a dispute that has followed Ali G for years: who is the audience really laughing at?

In 2000, comic Felix Dexter argued that Ali G let white middle-class viewers laugh at Black culture while still feeling free of racism.

NewsCord is a site that uses AI to compare news reports and flag bias. The site also helps readers send protest letters. Its Ali G campaign urges chains to refuse “Ali G: Who Iz I?” rather than sell tickets to what it views as racial mockery. The group has also asked Britain’s film ratings board how it judged the film’s racial jokes.

Its case goes back to Black British comics who spoke out years ago. It also cites complaints about Cohen’s other roles. It treats the new movie as part of that wider record, not a joke that can be judged only by what its creator says he meant.

Terry Gross put that same question to Cohen in 2007: did Borat’s jokes expose hatred of Jews or help it spread?

Cohen argued that Borat’s views were too wild to be taken as truth. The character thought Jews could turn into bugs. His aim, he told Gross, was to show how false such views were, not ask fans to share them.

His Jewish roots came up in their chat, too. “I’m proud to be a Jew,” Cohen said. He kept some customs out of that pride, though he said he was not religious.

But his concern went beyond people who held those views. When a bar crowd sang along with Borat’s anti-Jewish song, Cohen saw a danger in how easily they joined in. They did not have to hate Jews to help hate spread, he argued. They could simply go along with the song instead of speaking up or walking out.

For Cohen, Ali G’s joke lay in the gap between who he was and who he wanted to be. Cohen told Gross that Ali G saw himself as a Black Hip-Hop star from a tough part of town, though his home was a leafy suburb.

The dispute reached Druski’s team-up with Ali G earlier this month, which drew complaints about how the act used Black culture.

“Ali G: Who Iz I?” is due in U.K. theaters October 23.

Photo: DisclaimerBFILFF101024 (20 of 113) by Raph_PH, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0. Cropped and resized from original.

item.title: Shawty Dred Faces 63 Federal Counts Over Alleged $4 Million SNAP Scheme
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Shawty Dred faced 63 federal counts in an alleged $4 million SNAP scheme. Prosecutors announced the case on October 21.
item.content:encoded:
Shawty Dred was accused of using stolen identities and hundreds of food-benefit accounts to siphon about $4 million from SNAP, federal prosecutors announced on October 21.

The Atlanta rapper and social media personality, whose legal name is Mercedes Reshard New, was indicted on October 7 and arrested in Las Vegas on October 13. The 39-year-old faces 46 counts of mail fraud, 15 counts of aggravated identity theft and one count each of SNAP fraud and illegal transactions with access devices.

“New allegedly stole over $4 million meant for poor families who need help putting food on the table,” U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg said in the release.

In its announcement, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia described a scheme that allegedly ran from January 2020 through July 2026. Prosecutors said Shawty Dred controlled more than 350 fraudulent SNAP accounts opened with stolen identities and had benefit cards mailed to addresses around metro Atlanta.

SNAP, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, helps low-income households buy food. Georgia recipients receive benefits on electronic benefit transfer cards, known as EBT cards, which they can use at approved stores. Selling or trading those benefits is prohibited.

Prosecutors said Shawty Dred applied to make his company, Shawty Dred LLC, an approved SNAP retailer. They alleged that he then used fraudulently obtained cards and the company’s payment device to take more than $660,000 in benefits between April 2024 and November 2025.

The Agriculture Department revoked the store’s authorization in November 2025. About two weeks later, local officers arrested Shawty Dred on suspicion of selling SNAP benefits and seized 14 cards issued to other people, prosecutors said. They alleged that he then arranged to have replacement cards sent to his store and other Atlanta-area addresses.

Investigators also examined heavy use of the phone system that SNAP recipients use to access their accounts. In a separate national announcement, the Justice Department said phone numbers linked to Shawty Dred contacted that system more than 9,000 times and accessed over 350 accounts.

The local prosecutors’ announcement put the total transferred into allegedly fraudulent accounts at about $4.6 million, with roughly $4 million siphoned from those accounts.

Prosecutors also pointed to social media posts showing private jets, luxury cars and stacks of cash as they accused him of funding an extravagant lifestyle with benefits meant for food.

The charges are allegations, not findings of guilt. Shawty Dred is presumed innocent, and prosecutors must prove their case beyond a reasonable doubt.

Shawty Dred was remanded to U.S. Marshals Service custody pending further proceedings, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office. Its announcement did not identify a defense lawyer or include a response from him.

item.title: Diddy Back In General Population At New Prison After Being A “Bad Boy”
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Last week, the Bureau of Prisons confirmed Diddy's transfer from FCI Fort Dix in New Jersey to FCI Allenwood Low in Pennsylvania.
item.content:encoded:
TMZ reported Diddy was in Allenwood’s general population, citing union secretary Jose Rojas. His spokesman welcomed it if accurate.

AllHipHop has not independently verified his housing assignment.

The music executive, Sean “Diddy” Combs, moved from FCI Fort Dix in New Jersey to FCI Allenwood Low in Pennsylvania last week. The Bureau of Prisons confirmed that transfer to ABC News on October 16. That confirmation identified his prison, not his housing unit within it.

The bureau also told ABC News that privacy, safety and security concerns prevented it from discussing individual conditions of confinement or reasons for a transfer. Diddy’s representative acknowledged the move but said placement decisions belonged to the bureau and declined to explain the circumstances.

The Associated Press previously reported Diddy entered special housing at Fort Dix and lost 41 days of good-conduct credit.

Federal rules define a Special Housing Unit as a place where inmates are kept apart from the general population. They can be held alone or with others.

He is serving a 50-month sentence imposed in October 2025 after jurors convicted him of two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution. He was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy and sex trafficking.

When the transfer was announced last week, his representative told ABC News, “Sean remains focused on moving forward, and we hope that his time at the new facility will be productive and without unnecessary disruption.”

item.title: Floyd Mayweather Is Apparently Ready To Risk Everything Against Ryan Garcia
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: Ryan Garcia claims Floyd Mayweather has agreed to risk his perfect 50-0 record in a WBC welterweight championship fight, but major questions remain.
item.content:encoded:
Ryan Garcia just announced that Floyd Mayweather has agreed to put his legendary undefeated record on the line in a championship fight, and boxing fans have every reason to question whether this is actually happening.

The reigning WBC welterweight champion dropped the unexpected announcement Wednesday (October 21), claiming he and the retired boxing icon have reached an agreement to fight at 147 pounds.

“Floyd and I agree to a fight.

147 for the WBC welterweight championship of the world 🏆

50-0 vs The current champ”

Now, somebody explain how we got here!

Mayweather is 49 years old, hasn’t participated in an official professional fight since defeating Conor McGregor in 2017 and has spent much of his retirement collecting checks from exhibition bouts.

Garcia, meanwhile, is 28, holds the WBC welterweight championship and recently demolished Conor Benn in September. He is operating in his athletic prime while Mayweather is approaching his 50th birthday.

That is a 21-year age difference, ladies and gentlemen.

But there is something potentially historic about this peculiar proposition.

Mayweather retired with an immaculate 50-0 professional record. Garcia has repeatedly insisted that he isn’t interested in an exhibition. He wants a legitimate fight where Mayweather’s cherished undefeated record is actually vulnerable.

And apparently, according to Garcia, Floyd has agreed.

Earlier this month, reports surfaced that the two camps were discussing a possible showdown. Garcia subsequently challenged Mayweather publicly, questioning whether the boxing legend would risk his perfect record.

Interestingly, WBC president Mauricio Sulaiman has indicated that the organization could support such a fight if Mayweather passes the necessary medical examinations and receives approval from the appropriate boxing commission.

That doesn’t mean the championship fight has officially been sanctioned.

As of Wednesday evening, Mayweather has not publicly confirmed Garcia’s announcement. There is no announced date, venue, broadcaster or signed contract.

We have Garcia’s declaration, but several substantial questions remain unanswered.

There’s also something else that we have think about.

Remember what happened with the proposed Floyd Mayweather and Manny Pacquiao rematch? The two boxing legends generated considerable excitement about another showdown, but the anticipated fight never materialized.

That situation should serve as a reminder that boxing announcements, negotiations and actual fights are three very different things. Mayweather knows how to generate attention without necessarily stepping into the ring. So, while Garcia sounds confident, we’ve heard big promises involving Floyd before. Until contracts are signed and the fighters actually enter the ring, a healthy dose of skepticism is warranted.

Now think about this.

Would Mayweather genuinely jeopardize the undefeated record that helped define his career? Could a nearly 50-year-old defensive genius neutralize Garcia’s speed and punching power? And how much money would it take to convince Floyd that this gamble makes financial sense?

Remember, this is a man who turned boxing into an extraordinary business enterprise.

Personally, I need to see Mayweather acknowledge this arrangement before I start clearing my calendar.

Nevertheless, if Garcia is telling the truth, boxing could be preparing for one of its strangest championship spectacles.

Would you pay to see this?

item.title: Pusha T Never Expected “The Birds Don’t Sing” To Reach Beyond His Own Grief
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Pusha T reflected on the pain behind "The Birds Don't Sing" after being asked about families using the Clipse song at funerals.
item.content:encoded:
Pusha T wrote about losing his parents without expecting other grieving families to find a place for that pain in their own lives.

In a new ABC News interview, Linsey Davis asked him about people using Clipse’s “The Birds Don’t Sing” at funerals. Had he imagined the record becoming more than a personal expression?

“Never,” Pusha T replied.

He went back to what making the song had meant to him, his brother Malice and their longtime collaborator Pharrell Williams. The brothers’ parents died four months apart, and the people helping turn those losses into music knew the family long before the sessions began.

Pusha T explained that he and Pharrell grew up together, adding, “our families are intertwined.” That shared history made the recording personal for more than the two brothers behind the microphone.

He described the emotion among those making the record and those listening in the studio. “It was a very tough record to make,” he said.

The song opened “Let God Sort Em Out,” Clipse’s 2025 reunion album, with John Legend and the gospel choir Voices of Fire joining the brothers.

Pusha T addressed their mother in his verse, while Malice turned to their father. Before listeners reached the album’s street stories and rivalries, they heard the brothers work through their family’s grief.

That opening position was deliberate.

In an earlier GQ interview, Pusha T recalled people crying through the sessions and needing breaks. Rather than save the song for the album’s final stretch, the brothers decided it should introduce the project.

Malice had initially doubted they would finish it because writing about their parents stirred up so much. He later described the process as therapy. Looking at his own grandchildren also helped him understand the responsibility their father had carried, giving him a new way to think about those memories.

Malice had hoped it could do that. While discussing the song before the album’s release, he explained that honoring their parents also meant reliving his own grief with each line.

“Everyone is familiar with loss of some sort, and hopefully this can serve as healing for them as well,” Malice told Interview.

item.title: 50 Cent May Have Finally Met His Match In Tia Kemp
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: 50 Cent reportedly enlisted his lawyers after Tia Kemp targeted his son Sire, escalating their explosive social media feud into a potential legal battle.
item.content:encoded:
50 Cent may have finally encountered somebody who can match his legendary appetite for confrontation, and her name is Tia Kemp.

The ongoing feud between the G-Unit mogul and Rick Ross‘ former girlfriend has may have entered legal territory. According to a circulating video report, 50 Cent’s attorneys sent Kemp a cease and desist letter after she posted a photograph of his young son, Sire Jackson, accompanied by deeply personal insults.

Can we acknowledge the irony here?

50 Cent has practically built a second career out of humiliating his adversaries on social media. His Instagram account is a rough and tumble digital battlefield where everybody from rival rappers to their relatives can become collateral damage. He scares the mess outta me.

But apparently, there are limits when the shoe is on the other foot.

The latest fireworks started after Rick Ross’ son, William Roberts III, was allegedly pistol whipped and threatened near Bethune-Cookman University in Daytona Beach, Florida.

Rather than offering sympathy, 50 Cent mocked the situation and reportedly offered to post bond for the suspect.

Kemp, who shares William with Ross, was understandably furious. She responded by targeting 50 Cent and his son, Sire, including offensive remarks about the child’s development. We will not repeat her words. They were HARSH.

That apparently prompted the alleged legal intervention.

Kemp subsequently posted what was described as a cease and desist letter and unleashed another blistering social media tirade.

“Simpender about that one, huh? 50 f you and your lawyers. We got ours too.”

She was even more defiant during a livestream.

“Sending the crackers on me now. Want me to shut up when I get on that little chong, ain’t it?”

She also said Fif used a double standard when it comes to bringing children into public disputes. And is a legitimate question.

Can somebody who routinely weaponizes social media against his enemies suddenly demand boundaries when the retaliation becomes personal? His son is a minor and I get that. A mother does not care about nothing like that though.

Sire should not become ammunition in a dispute between adults. Neither should William, a student, whose reported assault involved law enforcement.

Earlier this year, 50 Cent criticized Rick Ross for pursuing a cease and desist against Remy Ma. Now, according to this latest account, his own attorneys are using similar tactics.

For the record, AllHipHop has not independently authenticated the purported letter. All there is what was partially posted by Tia Kemp.

Still, if the document proves legitimate, this feud has crossed from Instagram insults into legal consequences.

And Tia Kemp ain’t playing. I think RR knows she’s a beast.

Maybe 50 Cent has…his defining enemy.

item.title: Stephen A. Smith Says Phone Was Banned As Backlash Over Dinner With Trump Continues
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Stephen A. Smith cited a White House phone ban after Charlamagne Tha God called for a public record of his Trump dinner.
item.content:encoded:
Stephen A. Smith said he had to put his phone away before his dinner with Donald Trump. That was his answer to Charlamagne Tha God’s call for a public record of the White House visit.

The ESPN host addressed the point on “Straight Shooter” on October 20. He said he learned about the phone rule at the gate and handed his phone to his bodyguard.

“Would you have preferred that I turned around and not attend the meeting?” Smith asked.

For Charlamagne, the issue was who got to shape the story after dinner. On “The Breakfast Club”, he argued that media figures should speak with Trump on the record. That way, viewers could judge the exchange for themselves.

He wasn’t against the meeting itself. He wanted to see the guests press Trump, not just hear their accounts later. With no record to watch, he said, people were left to ask why the guests went and what they hoped to gain.

“I don’t want to just hear it from you after the fact. I want to see it,” he said.

Smith said Bill Maher, Maher’s executive producer and Kid Rock also had to give up their phones.

He said he respected Charlamagne and “The Breakfast Club” and had called him before the visit. He didn’t view their critique as a personal attack. Smith said he, too, would have liked to record the exchange.

The two had spoken about Trump before. In March 2024, Smith told Charlamagne he wouldn’t vote for Trump due to his conduct. That was more than two years before the dinner.

The visit took place on October 15. On CNN the next night, Smith said he went to make a case for historically Black colleges and universities. He cited his role as an HBCU Week ambassador and the chance to speak to someone with power to help. He said the evening ran four hours and 20 minutes.

Smith told CNN he told Trump that firms feared giving to those schools because of his stance on diversity, equity and inclusion. He said Trump agreed to look into it, but had made no firm pledge. Smith also said he had pressed for proof of Trump’s upbeat view of the economy.

On October 21, the show played Smith’s answer. Charlamagne said he would have wanted a sit-down that the public could see. He would have sought an interview, not a private dinner chat. He said he wasn’t holding Smith to a higher standard than anyone else. But he noted that elected leaders had to speak to Trump.
